finding: The five unit kinds are implement, review-role, review-record, audit-role, audit-record. None of them repairs anything: nothing edits the spec in response to recorded review findings, nothing changes code in response to audit findings, and nothing decomposes a converged spec into tasks. As written the driver can only re-run role units over an unchanged artifact, so no review or audit round can ever go from findings to clean, and §10 test 2 ('the loop advances through implement, review and audit phases and stops with converged') cannot be written at all — there is no unit whose execution changes the predicate the next round evaluates.
suggestion: Add the missing kinds and pin what each ends in: a `review-resolve` unit (ends in the spec file updated and `tp review --resolve/--resolve-all` applied, Alone), an `audit-fix` unit (ends in a code change committed, Alone), and a `decompose` unit (ends in `tp import` having written tasks, Alone). State for each which command produces its brief and what durable write the driver re-reads to decide the unit succeeded.

finding: The five unit kinds cover only the review, implement and audit phases, but the resume oracle reports five phases (review, decompose, implement, audit, release). In the decompose phase the loop of §3.1 has no pending units, is not releasable, and step 6 loops — so an unattended run spins until a cap trips, and the same hole applies to any state where resume returns blockers rather than work. The spec never says what the driver does when next_units is empty and stop_reason is not converged.
suggestion: Either add a decompose unit kind (ends in an imported task file) or state explicitly that a phase with no unit kind stops the run with its own stop_reason (e.g. no-units / needs-operator), and define which resume field means releasable (phase == release, or an explicit boolean) so §3.1 step 2 is implementable without guessing.

finding: Test 3 requires each cap to produce its own `stop_reason` 'and leaves cycle state untouched'. That is false by construction for any cap that trips after an `implement` unit ran: the task is committed and closed, so cycle state has changed. It is also unclear whether an in-flight unit is killed when a wall-clock or budget cap trips (§3.1 step 6 checks caps only between iterations, but a single unit can outlive the wall clock).
suggestion: Reword to what is actually invariant — 'a cap never marks a phase converged, never records a round, and never closes a task that its own unit did not close' — and pin cap-check timing: caps evaluated only between iterations, in-flight children run to completion (or are terminated with signal X after Y seconds), and the resulting exit is recorded as <exit-code>.

finding: The `args` template defines `{max_turns}` and `{max_budget_usd}` as per-unit caps, and §2 row 6 credits §3.4 with 'bounds spend per unit'. But §7 defines only run-level fields (`run_max_units`, `run_max_wall_clock_seconds`, `run_max_budget_usd`, `run_max_unit_retries`), and §3.4 says the budget cap counts 'the run's accumulated spend'. There is no field a test can set to make `{max_turns}` or a per-unit `{max_budget_usd}` take a known value, so §10 test 12 ('runner templates resolve every placeholder') has no expected substitution to assert.
suggestion: Add `run_max_unit_turns` and `run_max_unit_budget_usd` to §7 with defaults and ranges, and say explicitly how each placeholder is substituted (including what `{max_budget_usd}` expands to when the value is 0/unbounded — omitted argument, literal 0, or usage error).

finding: The `args` template offers `{max_turns}` and `{max_budget_usd}` placeholders, and §2's prior-art row promises "§3.4 bounds spend per unit", but §7 defines only run-level fields (`run_max_units`, `run_max_wall_clock_seconds`, `run_max_budget_usd`, `run_max_unit_retries`). No field supplies a per-unit turn or budget value, and `run_max_budget_usd` defaults to 0 (unbounded) — so the default configuration bounds neither per-unit nor total spend, contradicting the lesson row that says unbounded spend is what this design answers. Test 12 ("templates resolve every placeholder") cannot pass for a placeholder with no source.
suggestion: Add `run_max_unit_turns` and `run_max_unit_budget_usd` to §7 with defaults and ranges, or delete the two placeholders and the §2 per-unit claim; reconsider whether an unbounded default is compatible with an unattended driver.

finding: The args template has a {prompt} placeholder but nothing in the spec produces a prompt. §4.1 gives each unit a brief_command — a command string, not prompt text. It is not stated whether the driver executes brief_command and substitutes its stdout (which sits uneasily with §3.1's rule that the driver reads only exit codes and disk state), whether {prompt} is a fixed per-kind instruction that tells the child to run brief_command itself, or where per-role review/audit prompt text comes from at all.
suggestion: Name the exact producer of {prompt} per unit kind: e.g. the driver writes a small kind-specific prompt (verbatim text given in the spec) whose only instruction is to run the unit's brief_command, and state that brief_command output is never read by the driver. Add the prompt text or its template file path to §3.2.

finding: The built-in claude template is specified as print mode with streaming JSON output and --permission-mode auto. Claude Code's --permission-mode does not accept auto (the values are default, acceptEdits, plan, bypassPermissions), so the template cannot be built as written and the implementer would have to pick a permission posture — precisely the security-relevant choice the spec should own for an unattended run.
suggestion: Name the exact flag string of the claude template, including the real permission-mode value chosen for unattended runs and why, plus the output-format flag, and note that this pairs with the §6.2 deny hook as the actual fence.

finding: 'A run stops for exactly one of these reasons' but no reason covers the state 'the phase has nothing pending and the cycle is not releasable' — which §4.1 explicitly admits exists (`next_units` is [] while `next_action` names a phase transition), and which is the normal state at the decompose boundary given no decompose unit kind exists. The loop in §3.1 would spin through steps 3-6 with zero units until a wall-clock or unit cap trips, and no test can distinguish that spin from progress.
suggestion: Add a `no-units` (or `needs-operator`) `stop_reason` for an empty `next_units` on a non-releasable cycle, and require the driver to stop immediately rather than re-poll. Also state whether the driver sleeps between iterations, so a test can bound iterations.

finding: `cap-budget` and the per-unit `spend` column in §3.5's run.json require a number the spec never sources. For the built-in `claude` template it would come from parsing the runner's streaming JSON; for an arbitrary `runner.cmd` (§3.2 makes the harness configuration, not a dependency) there is no spend channel at all. A test for `cap-budget` therefore has no fixture, and the built-in path sits uncomfortably against Non-Goal 6 ('the driver reads exit codes and disk state').
suggestion: Pin the spend channel: name the exact key the driver reads from the runner's structured output for each built-in template, state what `spend` is when a custom runner emits nothing (null, and the budget cap is inert with a warning), and note in Non-Goal 6 that structured runner telemetry is not prose.

finding: `cap-budget` requires the driver to accumulate per-unit spend, and §3.5's run row carries a `spend` field — but §3.4 says budget/turn caps are "the runner's own flags, passed through per unit rather than reimplemented", §3.5 says the driver never reads the runner's JSONL output, and §3.2 makes the runner an arbitrary `cmd`/`args`. There is no defined, runner-agnostic channel by which tp learns what a unit spent, so `cap-budget` and the `spend` column cannot be produced for anything but a hard-coded harness.
suggestion: Name the channel: either require the runner template to declare a spend-extraction rule (a JSON path into the streaming output, per template), or scope `cap-budget` to the built-in `claude` template and say the field is unavailable for custom runners; adjust the §3.5 "never reads these" wording to distinguish reading into agent context from parsing a single total.

finding: `cap-budget`, the per-unit `spend` column in `.tp/run.json` (§3.5) and "spend against each cap" in `tp run --status` all require the driver to know what a unit cost, but §3.1 step 5 says "The driver's only reading of the process itself is its exit code" and §3.5 says the driver "never reads these [jsonl logs] into any context". Under its own rules the driver has no source for spend, so `run_max_budget_usd` is a knob that can never fire and `spend` is a byte that can never be filled — and §3.4 separately says budget caps are "the runner's own flags, passed through per unit rather than reimplemented", which bounds a unit, not a run.
suggestion: Either name the one narrow exception (the driver parses only the terminal cost record of the child's streaming JSON, never its prose) and say what happens when a runner reports no cost, or delete run-level `run_max_budget_usd`/`cap-budget`/`spend` and keep budget purely per unit via `{max_budget_usd}`.

finding: `unit-failure` fires when 'a unit failed `run_max_unit_retries` times in a row', with the field defaulting to 1 and ranging 0-5. It is not pinned whether the count includes the first attempt: at the default, does a unit get one attempt or two? At 0 the phrase is degenerate — either the unit never runs, or it runs once and one failure stops the run, and both readings are defensible. `cap-budget` has the same problem in the other direction: §7 documents 0 as 'unbounded' but the §3.4 row says the run stops when spend 'reached run_max_budget_usd', which at 0 is true before the first unit.
suggestion: Say 'a unit is attempted 1 + run_max_unit_retries times; retries=0 means one attempt and no retry' and give the worked default. For the budget row, state the 0 exemption inline and use an explicit comparison ('accumulated spend >= run_max_budget_usd, and the cap is disabled when the resolved value is 0').

finding: cap-budget requires the driver to accumulate per-unit spend, and §3.5's run.json rows carry a spend column, but no source for that number is defined. §3.1 step 5 says the driver's only reading of the process is its exit code, and §3.5 says the driver never reads the .jsonl logs into any context. For a generic cmd runner there is no spend-reporting protocol at all. Additionally, with role units running in parallel and caps checked only between iterations, a batch of concurrent units can overshoot run_max_budget_usd before the next check.
suggestion: Specify the spend channel (e.g. the driver parses only the terminal result event of the runner's stream-json log for total_cost_usd; a runner with no such field reports spend 0 and cap-budget is inert for it), state that reading that one field is not prose parsing, and say whether the cap is checked before dispatch using a per-unit worst case or only after each iteration.

finding: §3.5 justifies `.tp/run.json` as "one git-ignored progress file that no decision reads back", but two decisions do read it back: §4.2 puts `last_failure` in the run state and has `tp resume`/`tp brief` surface it to the next unit, and §3.4's wall-clock and budget accruals cannot be re-derived from cycle state after a driver crash. So either the file is read back (and the stated justification is false, leaving the drift risk unaddressed) or those bytes are written and never consumed.
suggestion: Name the exact keys that are read back (`last_failure`, accrued totals) and state what happens to caps on a resume after a crash — do they restart at zero, and is that acceptable for an 8-hour default. Drop or derive the rest: the per-unit rows are already reconstructible from the `.tp/runs/<run-id>/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` filenames.

finding: §3.5 states run.json is 'observability, not truth' and that it is 'one git-ignored progress file that no decision reads back'. §4.2 then stores `last_failure` in that same run state and requires `tp resume` and `tp brief` to surface it to the next unit — which is precisely a decision-affecting read-back, and the one continuity the design says it needs. The two rules cannot both be tested: a test asserting 'nothing reads run.json' and a test asserting 'the next unit sees last_failure' contradict.
suggestion: Pick one and say it: either carve out `last_failure` explicitly ('run.json is not consulted for cycle state; `last_failure` is the single exception, and it is advisory — its absence never changes what the driver runs next'), or move `last_failure` to a location that is allowed to be read back and state whether it survives a driver crash.

finding: `next_units` re-encodes state `next_action` already carries. SKILL.md ships `next_action.brief_command` ("names the right command per phase") and `next_action.payload` ("embeds the next unit's work, so a fresh agent needs one call"), so `next_units[].brief_command` is a second copy of a shipped field and `next_units` as a whole is a second copy of the same decision. Every fresh unit reads `tp resume --json` at start, so the duplicated array is paid on every single unit of an unattended run, and the two representations must be kept in sync forever.
suggestion: Either define `next_units` as the sole machine surface and reduce `next_action` to a rendering of `next_units[0]` (stating that `brief_command` now lives in exactly one place), or drop `next_units` and extend `next_action` with a `concurrent_with` list. State which field an agent parses and which is prose.

finding: §3.1 step 2 and §3.4 both key the run's only success exit on 'the cycle is releasable' / 'the oracle reports the cycle releasable', but no field is named that a test can assert. §4.1 then says 'next_action.kind names the phase transition' — `next_action` has no `kind` member; its documented shape is {command, brief_command, summary, payload} (skills/tp/REFERENCE.md). Two engineers will write two different releasability assertions (one on `next_action.command == null`, one on a `kind` field that does not exist).
suggestion: Name the exact observable: e.g. 'the cycle is releasable iff `tp resume --json` reports <field> == "release" and `next_units` is []'. Either add `kind` to `next_action` as an explicit, enumerated new field in this spec (and list it in §10.1 as a shape change), or reference the existing member that carries the phase.

finding: last_failure is recorded in the run state, yet §3.5 says the run state is observability only and that no decision reads it back, while §4.2 requires tp resume and tp brief — separate processes, possibly in the next run — to read it back and surface it. Since .tp/run.json is per-run and a new run re-derives everything from cycle state, a failure from the previous run is either lost or the run file becomes a second source of truth. The implementer cannot choose a store from the spec.
suggestion: Pick one: keep last_failure in a small cycle-scoped file (e.g. .tp/last_failure.json, git-ignored) that outlives a run, and amend §3.5 to say run.json holds only per-run rows/totals; or state that last_failure is run-scoped and explicitly not carried across runs. Also define its lifetime when the failing unit never runs again.

finding: §4.2 stores `last_failure` in the run state (`.tp/run.json`) and has `tp resume`/`tp brief` read it back to brief the next unit — but §3.5 declares that file "observability, not truth", git-ignored, and explicitly "one git-ignored progress file that no decision reads back". Worse, §3.5 promises the next `tp run` re-derives everything from cycle state after a driver death, which would silently drop the one piece of continuity §4.2 calls genuinely necessary. Two sections give the same file opposite contracts.
suggestion: Pick one: either persist `last_failure` in the durable cycle state (`.tp-review/` or the task file, which is where `tp resume` already derives from) and leave `.tp/run.json` read-never, or amend §3.5 to name `last_failure` as the single exception, state that it survives driver death, and say what happens when the run file is missing.

finding: Row 2 of the fail-closed table refuses `tp set --workflow review_max_rounds=`/`audit_max_rounds=` only when it is 'raising a cap', so lowering or setting an equal value is presumably still allowed — but §10 test 8 asserts flatly that 'each of the three user-only operations exits 2 with its hint'. The two cannot both be implemented. It is also unpinned what the new value is compared against (the resolved value, the project-config value, or the task-file override) and whether a direct hand-edit of `.tp/config.json` under TP_UNATTENDED is covered.
suggestion: State the comparison explicitly ('rejected when the requested value exceeds the currently resolved value; equal or lower is accepted, exit 0'), and rewrite test 8 to cover all three arms: raise → exit 2, lower → exit 0, and the same raise without the variable → exit 0. Say whether config-file writes are in scope (they are outside tp's CLI, so probably not — but say so).

finding: The claim that the escape hatch is unreachable does not hold as specified. TP_UNATTENDED is an env var the child can drop (env -u TP_UNATTENDED tp done --skip-gate ...), and the round caps the guard protects live in .tp/config.json, which the §6.2 deny list does not cover — it denies only .tp-review/ contents and *.tasks.json. An agent can raise review_max_rounds/audit_max_rounds by editing the config file directly, or add run_max_units, or point runner/notify_cmd at anything.
suggestion: Add .tp/config.json (and .tp/local.json) to the PreToolUse deny list, state that the three refusals are enforced on the resolved value regardless of how it is reached, and either drop the unreachability claim or back it with a hook-level deny on env-stripping invocations. State explicitly whether lowering a cap is still permitted while raising is refused.

finding: `tp run` sets `TP_UNATTENDED=1` for every child, while §3.2 lets `runner.env` supply 'extra environment for the child, merged over the parent's'. Precedence is not pinned, so an operator (or a future generated config) can set TP_UNATTENDED=0 in `runner.env` and silently reopen every escape hatch §5.1 exists to close. Also unpinned: whether values other than the literal `1` (empty, `0`, `true`) activate the mode, which a test must know to assert the boundary.
suggestion: State that `TP_UNATTENDED` is applied after the `runner.env` merge and cannot be overridden by it (or that an attempt to set it in `runner.env` is a usage error), and define activation precisely — e.g. 'active when the variable is present and non-empty and not "0"'.

finding: §5.1 guarantees user-only decisions are "unreachable while unattended" because `tp run` sets `TP_UNATTENDED=1` for every child, but §3.2 defines `runner.env` as "Extra environment for the child, merged over the parent's" — a config-supplied env wins over the driver's own variable, so the fail-closed fence can be turned off by the very configuration an unattended unit is able to edit.
suggestion: State in §3.2 that `TP_UNATTENDED` (and any other driver-owned variable) is applied after the `env` merge and cannot be overridden or unset, and add a test to §10 asserting a `runner.env` entry for `TP_UNATTENDED` does not reach the child.

finding: An escalating unit 'exits 2', but 2 is tp's generic usage-error code (skills/tp/REFERENCE.md §13) and §10 test 12 assigns it again to an unresolved runner placeholder. The driver therefore cannot distinguish 'the agent asked for a user-only decision' from 'the agent typed a bad flag' without reading the message — which is exactly the defect §8a raises and this section is a fresh instance of. Test 9 and test 12 assert the same observable for opposite intents.
suggestion: Give escalation a distinct signal a driver can branch on without prose: either a dedicated exit code, or make the escalation record's existence the discriminator and say so ('exit 2 plus an escalation record written this run = escalation; exit 2 with no record = usage failure, counted as a unit failure').

finding: An escalation is detected as a unit that exits 2 and writes an escalation record, but the record has no path, no schema and no named writer (the refusing tp command, or the agent?), and exit 2 is already tp's usage-error code — the same code §5.1 assigns to the three refusals and the same code the harness itself may return for a bad invocation. There is also no stated mechanism by which the inner tp exit code becomes the child agent process's exit code: an agent harness typically exits 0 after a failed inner command.
suggestion: Define the escalation record path and JSON fields (e.g. .tp/escalation.json with {decision, evidence, options, unit_kind, unit_id, at}), make the record's presence — not the exit code — the escalation signal, and say what the driver does with an exit 2 that has no record (unit failure). If the exit code must carry meaning, state how the child is required to propagate it.

finding: The escalation record — 'naming the decision, the evidence, and what it would do with each answer' — has no path, no file format, no field names, and no statement of who writes it (the unit, or the driver on seeing exit 2). §10 test 9 asserts an escalating unit 'stops the run with artifacts intact', which cannot be written without knowing which artifact to assert on.
suggestion: Pin the path (e.g. `.tp/runs/<run-id>/escalation.json` or a field inside run.json), the exact keys ({decision, unit_kind, unit_id, phase, evidence, options[], at}), the writer, and whether more than one escalation can accumulate in a run.

finding: §5.2 makes an escalating unit exit 2, but 2 is already tp's usage-error code and is also what §5.1's blocked operations return; meanwhile §3.1 fixes "the driver's only reading of the process itself is its exit code" and §3.4/§4.2 count any non-zero exit as a unit failure that records `last_failure` and retries. So the driver cannot distinguish escalation (`stop_reason: escalation`, normal outcome) from a usage error or a crashed unit, and §8a's own routed finding is that exit codes already fail to separate a typo from a failure — this section adds a third meaning to the same code. The spec also never says where the escalation record is written or in what format the driver detects it.
suggestion: Either allocate a distinct exit code for escalation (and update the exit-code table explicitly, since §10.1 currently claims no codes change) or define detection by the presence of a named escalation file at a specified path, and state in §3.4/§4.2 that an escalation exit is not counted as a unit failure and does not set `last_failure`.

finding: The `PreToolUse` deny is scoped to 'file-writing tools' without enumerating them, and the denied set includes `*.tasks.json` — a file tp's own commands (`tp done`, `tp import`, `tp commit`) rewrite, which the unit invokes through a shell tool. If shell tools are in the matcher the fence breaks every close; if they are not, `sed -i` walks straight through the fence. No test can be written until the matcher set is named.
suggestion: List the exact tool names in the matcher and state the shell case explicitly — e.g. 'matches Write, Edit, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit; shell commands are out of scope by design, because the fence exists to stop hand-editing, not to sandbox, and tp's own writes must pass'.

finding: The scope fence in §6.2 denies writes only to `.tp-review/` contents and `*.tasks.json`, while §5.1 blocks the round-cap escape hatch only at the `tp set --workflow` CLI. Nothing stops an unattended unit from editing `.tp/config.json` directly to raise `review_max_rounds`/`audit_max_rounds` — which is exactly the "agent raises its own round budget and then declares convergence" forgery §5.1 names as the countermeasure's target. The block is at the entry point, not at the sink (CLAUDE.md's own rule).
suggestion: Extend the §6.2 PreToolUse denial to `.tp/config.json` (and any file holding workflow policy) under `TP_UNATTENDED=1`, or have the oracle re-read the round caps from a value recorded at run start and treat a mid-run increase as an escalation.

finding: §6.3 declares `tp-reviewer` and `tp-auditor` 'read-only with respect to the repository', but §3.3 requires each role unit to end in a durable write — 'one role's findings file for the round'. The spec never says where that file lives, and the only documented home for round artifacts, `.tp-review/`, is denied to every writing tool by §6.2. Three sections describe three incompatible permissions for the same write, so no test can assert that a reviewer unit succeeds.
suggestion: Pin the findings-file path for role units (e.g. `.tp/runs/<run-id>/<seq>-<role>.ndjson`, outside `.tp-review/` and git-ignored), and restate the reviewer/auditor restriction as 'may write only its own findings file' rather than 'read-only with respect to the repository'.

finding: None of the four field-carried defects §8a says 'this release must answer' has a test row in §10: no test for an honest (clustered) finding count, none for `next_action` no longer recommending an unhonourable check registration, none for a truncated audit reporting its true total, none for the exit-code split. §10.1 additionally asserts 'no existing command's exit codes change outside TP_UNATTENDED=1', which the §8a exit-code item directly contradicts once it is folded in.
suggestion: Add one test row per §8a item when each is folded into its owning section, and update §10.1 to name the arity-violation exit-code change and the existing assertions it invalidates.

finding: §10.1 asserts "No existing command's exit codes change outside `TP_UNATTENDED=1`", but §8a routes an exit-code defect this release "must answer" (arity violations exit 1 where an unknown command exits 2), and §5.2 introduces escalation as a new meaning for exit 2. Any of those fixes changes existing exit codes in the attended path and invalidates tests §10.1 says are untouched.
suggestion: Once the §8a exit-code finding is folded into a numbered section, update §10.1 to list the commands whose codes move and the tests that pin them; if the fix is deferred, say so explicitly in §9 Non-Goals instead of leaving §10.1's claim standing.

finding: Only --status and --dry-run are given. Whether tp run takes a spec argument like tp resume [spec] or relies on discovery, whether -f/--file applies, and whether the new caps have CLI flags are unstated — yet §7 says these fields resolve through the layered path whose highest precedence is CLI, which implies flags that no section defines. The review phase also needs a spec path to pass to tp review, and it is not said where the driver gets it.
suggestion: Give tp run's full argument and flag surface, including the CLI overrides implied by §7's precedence chain (or state that these fields have no CLI layer), and name the field of the resume payload the driver uses as the spec path.

finding: 'the substitute must be equal or stronger, never cheaper' is written as a requirement ('must') in the same paragraph that says 'tp takes no position on which model to use — it has no way to know'. No pass/fail test can be written for a constraint the tool cannot evaluate, and a reader can reasonably conclude tp is supposed to validate the judge runner.
suggestion: Demote it to guidance and mark it as such ('tp does not and cannot enforce this; it is documented in SKILL.md as operator guidance'), or make it enforceable by pinning something tp can see (e.g. a warning when the audit runner is byte-identical to the implement runner).

finding: The built-in `claude` template is described only in prose — 'print mode with streaming JSON output, --permission-mode auto, and the per-unit turn and budget caps' — so the argv a test would assert against the `TP_RUNNER` fake cannot be derived from the spec. `--permission-mode auto` is also not one of the harness's documented permission-mode values, so an implementer copying the spec literally produces a runner that fails to start, and the reviewer has nothing to check the value against.
suggestion: Print both built-in templates as literal `cmd` + `args` arrays in the spec, so §10 test 12 asserts recorded argv against the spec text, and verify the permission-mode value against the harness's documented enum before pinning it.

finding: Two built-in templates ship by name, but only the claude one is described even partially; the opencode template has no cmd, no args, no output format, and no statement of how (or whether) it supports the turn cap, the budget cap and the §6.3 dynamic-agent path. A template that ships by name is a task nobody can implement or test from the spec.
suggestion: Give the opencode template's concrete cmd/args/env exactly as for claude, and state what happens for placeholders it cannot support (omit the flag, or reject the template with a usage error).

finding: `runner` is specified as three shapes at once — a built-in name, an object, or a map keyed by unit kind with `default` — and every consumer (`tp config --resolved`, `--extract`, `tp validate --project`, §7) must handle all three. The only motivation given is separating producer from judge, which needs two buckets, not five keys. The extra generality is knob surface an agent must learn and a validator must cover with no decision behind it.
suggestion: Narrow the map to the distinction actually argued: keys `default` and `judge` (covering `review-role`/`audit-role`), or a plain second field `runner_judge`. If per-kind keying is kept, name a real case where `implement` and `review-record` need different runners.

finding: runner is a three-way union — a built-in name string, an inline object, or a map keyed by unit kind with a default key whose values are themselves name-or-object — but §7 describes it only as 'Built-in name or object'. The parse rules, the precedence when both a kind key and default match, the error for an unknown built-in name or an unknown unit-kind key, and how tp config --extract and tp validate --project render and check this shape are all left to the implementer.
suggestion: Give the JSON shape for all three forms with one example each, state the resolution rule (exact kind key > default > built-in default), and specify the validation errors with their exit codes.

finding: A `review-role`/`audit-role` unit's entire durable result is "one role's findings file for the round" (§3.3), and §3.1 step 5 defines a unit's result as what it wrote to disk — but §6.2 denies writes to `.tp-review/` contents from file-writing tools, and the spec never says where a role's findings file lives. If it lives under `.tp-review/` the fence blocks the only write the unit exists to make; if it lives elsewhere, the driver has no stated path at which to find it before the record unit runs.
suggestion: Name the findings-file path convention in §3.3 (e.g. `.tp/runs/<run-id>/…` or a role-scoped subdirectory) and state in §6.2 that the denial covers recorded round state but not the round's in-flight role files, or route role writes through a tp subcommand so the file-write fence is not in the path.

finding: review-role and audit-role units end in 'one role's findings/results file for the round', but the file's location and name are never given — and if that location is under .tp-review/, the §6.2 PreToolUse hook denies exactly the write the unit exists to make. The record unit then has to find those files to merge them, so the path is load-bearing for two kinds.
suggestion: State the per-role output path the driver hands each unit and the record unit consumes (e.g. an out-of-tree run directory, or a named subpath excluded from the deny rule), and make the deny rule's exclusion explicit so the two sections cannot be implemented in conflict.

finding: The caps table bounds the run's units, wall clock and budget, and §3.4 says turn and budget caps are the runner's own flags, but nothing bounds a single unit's wall clock inside the driver. A child that stalls (a hung tool, a runner that ignores its turn cap, an interactive prompt despite closed stdin) blocks the loop indefinitely, and the wall-clock cap can only trip between iterations, so it never fires.
suggestion: Add a per-unit timeout (a workflow field with a default, or the remaining wall-clock budget) after which the driver kills the child and counts a unit failure, and state that the wall-clock cap is also enforced against in-flight units, not only at iteration boundaries.

finding: `unit-failure` trips when "a unit failed `run_max_unit_retries` times in a row", but the field is named for retries, not failures, and §7 gives it default 1 and range 0-5. With the default, one failure either stops the run immediately (no retry ever happens, making the name wrong) or allows two attempts (making §3.4's sentence wrong); with 0 the stop condition is either vacuous or unreachable. A driver's most common branch is decided by this sentence.
suggestion: State attempts explicitly: "a unit is attempted 1 + `run_max_unit_retries` times; when the last attempt fails the run stops with `unit-failure`", and give the 0 case its own sentence.

finding: run_max_unit_retries default 1 with stop condition 'a unit failed run_max_unit_retries times in a row' conflates retries with attempts — 1 could mean stop after the first failure or after one re-attempt (two runs). It is also unstated whether 'in a row' is per unit id or across the run, whether a retry re-spawns with the same prompt and a fresh process, and what happens to partial durable writes from the failed attempt (a claimed wip task, a half-written findings file) before the retry.
suggestion: State attempts = retries + 1, scope the streak to a single unit id, say the retry is a fresh process with the same prompt, and specify whether the driver cleans or tolerates partial writes (e.g. a role file is overwritten; a wip task is left claimed and resumed).

finding: stop_reason interrupted says only that the operator signalled the driver. Which signals are handled, whether in-flight children are killed or waited out, whether a second signal force-quits, and what happens to a unit killed mid-write (a partially written task file under flock, a half-written role file) are all undefined — and test 3 asserts every cap leaves cycle state untouched, which an interrupt must also satisfy.
suggestion: Name the handled signals (SIGINT/SIGTERM), specify graceful drain of in-flight children with a bounded wait then kill, state that run state records interrupted after the drain, and say what the driver does with partial artifacts.

finding: Nothing prevents two tp run processes over the same repo. Both would derive the same pending units from resume, spawn duplicate implement units against the same task, and interleave writes to .tp/run.json and .tp/runs/. Every other write path in tp takes a flock; the driver — the longest-lived writer of all — has no stated exclusion, and test 6's crash-recovery case needs to distinguish a stale run from a live one.
suggestion: Require the driver to hold an exclusive lock (e.g. flock on .tp/run.lock) for the duration of the run, define the second driver's error and exit code, and define how a stale lock/run from a crashed driver is detected and reclaimed.

finding: Test 6 requires that a second tp run over the same state resumes at the same unit, but a crashed implement unit typically leaves a claimed wip task plus uncommitted edits, which is exactly the state resume reports as unexplained changes/blockers rather than as pending work. The spec never says how the driver treats a resume payload that carries blockers: proceed, stop, or escalate.
suggestion: Define the driver's blocker policy explicitly — e.g. any blocker in the resume payload stops the run with its own stop_reason and a report — and state whether a wip task from a crashed unit is re-dispatched as the same implement unit or requires operator action.

finding: run.json is described in prose ('the run id, start time, one row per executed unit (kind, id, exit code, duration, spend, log path), the accrued totals, and stop_reason') with no JSON key names, no types, no unit for duration, and no format for the run id or the `<seq>` component of the log path. §3.5 also describes a single current run, while §10 test 11 asserts `--status` 'reports an in-flight run, a converged run and each stopped run' — implying retained history the file shape does not provide.
suggestion: Give the literal JSON skeleton with key names and types (`run_id`, `started_at`, `units[]` with `exit_code`, `duration_ms`, `spend_usd`, `log_path`, plus `totals` and `stop_reason`), fix the seq format (zero-padded width), and say whether run.json is overwritten per run or holds the last N — then align test 11 with that answer.

finding: `next_units[].concurrent` stores what §3.3's table already fixes statically: role kinds are parallel, record and implement kinds are alone. Nothing in the spec makes concurrency vary per unit, so the boolean is a stored derivation emitted on every unit of every resume call, and it creates a second place the concurrency rule can be wrong.
suggestion: Drop `concurrent` and have the driver derive concurrency from `kind`; or, if per-unit variance is actually intended, say what varies it (§9.5 suggests nothing does).

finding: `next_units` entries carry `brief_command` (§4.1) while the runner template consumes a `{prompt}` placeholder (§3.2). Nothing states how one becomes the other — whether the driver executes `brief_command` and substitutes its stdout (which puts the brief in the driver's memory, in tension with §3.1's "never holds work in memory it could re-derive"), or passes the command itself for the child to run. Test 12 asserts placeholder resolution without a defined source for the largest placeholder.
suggestion: Specify the mapping in §3.2 or §4.1: e.g. `{prompt}` is a short instruction naming `brief_command` for the child to run as its first call, so the brief never transits the driver — and say what happens when `brief_command` fails.

finding: next_units entries carry an id, but the id namespace is never defined. Three separate behaviours depend on it: last_failure clears when a unit with the same id next succeeds, unit-failure counts retries for the same unit, and the log path embeds <id>. If a review-role unit's id is the role name, a later round's success clears an earlier round's failure; if it embeds the round, the failure can never be cleared. Path-unsafe characters in a task id are also unaddressed.
suggestion: Give the id grammar per kind (e.g. implement:<task-id>, review-role:<round>:<role>, review-record:<round>) plus the character set allowed in a log filename, and say which component last_failure and retry counting key on.

finding: `last_failure.summary` is free text with no stated source. The only thing available on a non-zero exit is the child's natural-language output, and §9.6 forbids exactly that ("It never infers status from a unit's natural-language output"). The field is also injected into the next unit's context by `tp resume`/`tp brief`, so an unbounded prose blob is paid in tokens by the retry. `phase` in the same object is fully derivable from `unit_kind` per §3.3.
suggestion: Define `summary` as a bounded, non-prose value (exit code + failing command + log path, or the quality-gate's own last lines) with a stated char cap, or replace it with a `log_path` pointer. Drop `phase` and derive it from `unit_kind`.

finding: `last_failure` is a single object, but its clearing rule is per-id: 'cleared when a unit with the same id next succeeds'. If unit A fails and then unit B fails, A's record is overwritten and can never be cleared by its own rule; if B is overwritten by A's success, B's failure silently vanishes. The `at` timestamp has no pinned format, and `summary`'s source is unstated — if it is drawn from the unit's natural-language output it collides with Non-Goal 6.
suggestion: Either keep one object and clear it on any unit success (say so), or key it by unit id as a small map and pin the eviction rule. Pin `at` as RFC3339 and define `summary` as a driver-composed string from structured facts (kind, id, exit code, log path) rather than from the unit's text.

finding: Under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` all three refusals exit 2 with "a hint naming it a user-approved decision". That hint tells the agent to obtain user approval in the exact mode where no user is reachable — the same shape as the hint problem the repo just fixed ("stop hints that recommend the command that just refused"). The bytes are spent recommending an unavailable action instead of the available one (§5.2 escalation).
suggestion: Specify the unattended hint text to name the escalation path — write the escalation record and stop — rather than "ask the user". Add it to test 8's assertion so the two modes' hints are pinned apart.

finding: The escalation record is the one artifact that decides whether a stopped run is resumable by a human, yet the spec gives it no path, no schema and no reader. §3.5's `tp run --status` list does not mention it, so the operator returning to a stopped run gets `stop_reason: escalation` with no pointer to the decision, the evidence, or the branches. Test 9 asserts only "artifacts intact".
suggestion: Name the path (e.g. `.tp/runs/<run-id>/escalation.json`), the field set, and add it to what `tp run --status` prints when `stop_reason` is `escalation`. Tighten test 9 to assert the record's fields.

finding: `notify_cmd` has no execution contract: shell-interpreted or exec'd directly, what arguments or environment carry the escalation context, whether stdout/stderr are captured, what timeout bounds it, and what the run does if it exits non-zero or hangs. §10 test 9 asserts it 'is invoked' with no observable named. §7 types it 'Any command string', so `tp validate --project` has nothing to validate.
suggestion: Pin the invocation (e.g. `sh -c <string>` with TP_RUN_ID, TP_STOP_REASON, TP_ESCALATION_PATH in the environment), a timeout with a default, and the rule that a failing notify never changes `stop_reason`. Give the test a concrete observable — a fixture command that writes a file the assertion reads.

finding: The plugin 'preflights: if `tp` is absent from PATH or older than the plugin's minimum, it fails with the install command'. No minimum version is stated, no version-comparison rule is given (tp's `--version` string format is not referenced), and no channel is named for the failure — which hook runs it, and whether 'fails' means a blocking hook exit or a printed warning. §10 has no test for the preflight at all.
suggestion: State the minimum version literally (v0.35.0), pin the comparison (semver on the `tp --version` output, with an unparseable version treated as too old), name the hook that performs it and the blocking behaviour, and add a test row covering absent / too-old / acceptable.

finding: The Stop hook must know whether a unit is in flight, which kind it is, and whether anything durable was written, but the only environment the spec gives a child is TP_UNATTENDED=1. {unit_id} exists solely as an args placeholder, nothing carries the kind, and 'nothing durable was written' has a different meaning per kind (a commit, a closed task, a role file, a recorded round) that is never defined.
suggestion: Pass TP_UNIT_ID and TP_UNIT_KIND (and the run id) into every child, define the durable-write predicate per kind, and say whether the hook computes it itself or calls a tp subcommand that answers it.

finding: The `SessionStart` hook injects "the cycle's orientation" on every matcher, with the payload characterised only as "small". It fires for every session in the repo, including interactive sessions doing unrelated work and units whose very first call is `tp next --brief` (which returns the same orientation again). For a driver whose entire premise is that a unit begins with an empty context, an unbounded and undefined always-on prefix is the one thing that erodes it.
suggestion: Define the payload exactly (the `--compact` `tp resume` summary), give it a byte cap, and specify that it emits nothing when no active task file or no in-flight cycle exists. Add a test asserting the injected size ceiling.

finding: 'Runners that cannot load a plugin receive the same definitions through the runner template's dynamic-agent flag' names no flag, and gives no rule by which tp decides a runner cannot load a plugin — a built-in template property, a config field, or a probe. The claim that 'the role contract is identical in both paths' is the testable part, and it has no fixture: the agent definitions' contents (tools allowed, prompt) are never pinned.
suggestion: Name the flag per built-in template, add an explicit `supports_plugin` (or equivalent) property to the runner object for custom runners, and pin the three agent definitions' tool allowlists in the spec so a test can assert plugin-path and flag-path definitions are byte-equal.

finding: Review and audit role content already lives in the corpus (`.tp/reviewers/`, `.tp/auditors/`) and is emitted into the prompt by `tp review`/`tp audit`. §6.3 adds `agents/tp-reviewer` and `agents/tp-auditor`, plus a third path via "the runner template's dynamic-agent flag". That is three declarations of one role contract, and the spec asserts they are identical without saying which is the source. A role's instructions drifting between the plugin copy and the corpus copy is a defect no test in §10 catches.
suggestion: State that plugin/dynamic agents carry ONLY the tool restrictions (read-only fences) and that all role content continues to come from the corpus through the emitted prompt, so there is one source. Add a test asserting the plugin agents contain no role instructions.

finding: Runners that cannot load a plugin are said to receive the agent definitions through 'the runner template's dynamic-agent flag', but §3.2's placeholder list has no such placeholder, the flag is not named, and the serialization of an agent definition for that path (inline JSON? file path? which fields?) is unspecified. The implementer would have to invent the whole channel.
suggestion: Add the placeholder to §3.2's table, name the flag per built-in template, and give the agent-definition payload shape plus what happens when a runner supports neither plugin nor flag.

finding: §6.3 declares `tp-reviewer`/`tp-auditor` agents in the plugin and claims "the role contract is identical in both paths" via the runner template's dynamic-agent flag — but §3.2 makes the runner an arbitrary `cmd`/`args` with no such flag guaranteed, so the claim cannot hold for a custom runner. It also puts role definitions in a second place: since v0.25.0 the role corpus (`.tp/reviewers/`, `.tp/auditors/`) owns roles and `tp review`/`tp audit` emit their prompts, and §3.5 itself calls two sources of truth for one fact the drift to avoid.
suggestion: Say that the plugin agents carry only tool restrictions while the role prompt continues to come from the corpus via `tp review`/`tp audit`, and weaken the identical-in-both-paths claim to a documented degradation (custom runners get the corpus prompt without the tool fence) or make the dynamic-agent flag a declared requirement of a conforming runner template.

finding: 'Every hook the plugin ships declares a timeout and exits non-zero rather than hanging' gives no value, no default, and no range, so a fixture assertion ('the hook config declares timeout = N') cannot be written, and two implementers will pick different numbers. It is also unstated what the driver observes when a hook times out — whether the unit is a unit failure, a retry, or a silent continue.
suggestion: Pin a concrete timeout per hook (or one value for all three) in the section, and state the unit-level consequence of a hook timeout so §3.4's failure accounting is complete.

finding: The section claims the new fields resolve 'through the existing layered path', which REFERENCE pins as CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in — but §3.5 names only `--status` and `--dry-run` as flags, so no CLI layer exists for any of the six fields, and no env var names are given. Out-of-range behaviour is also unstated: REFERENCE says hand-edited out-of-range caps fall back to 0 at read time, which for `run_max_units` would silently mean a run that executes nothing. `runner`'s Range cell says 'Built-in name or object' and omits the per-unit-kind map form §3.2 introduces.
suggestion: List the CLI flags and env var names for each new field (or state that these fields have no CLI/env layer and that precedence starts at the task override), give the read-time fallback per field, and extend the `runner` range cell to cover the keyed-map form with `default`.

finding: `notify_cmd` is placed among project-level workflow defaults, i.e. committed `.tp/config.json`, but a notification command is per-operator and per-machine — every collaborator inherits one person's desktop notifier. tp already has the git-ignored layer for exactly this (`.tp/local.json` holds the active pointer, CLI `defaults`, and `keep_uncommitted`). It is also an arbitrary command string that a committed file makes executable for anyone who pulls.
suggestion: Move `notify_cmd` to `.tp/local.json` (or state that the local layer overrides it and that `tp config --extract` never emits it), and say what its exit code means to the run.

finding: notify_cmd is 'any command string' with no invocation contract: shell vs argv split, what arguments or environment carry the escalation context, whether stdout/stderr are captured or logged, what a non-zero exit or a hang does to the stopping run, and whether it fires for every non-converged stop or only escalation (§5.2 mentions it only there, §3.4 not at all). It is also arbitrary command execution driven from a committed config file that, per the §5.1 threat model, an unattended agent can currently write.
suggestion: Define the execution form (argv or sh -c), the context passed (env vars or a JSON payload on stdin), a timeout with a non-fatal failure policy, and which stop_reasons trigger it; and cover it under the config write fence.

finding: §3.2 says `.tp/config.json` gains a `runner` object, while §7 lists `runner` and `notify_cmd` as workflow fields resolving "through the existing layered path" — which by tp's documented precedence (CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in) makes both settable from a `<base>.tasks.json` workflow override and from the environment. Both fields are command-valued, so under that precedence an agent-writable layer chooses the executable the driver spawns and the command it runs on escalation, and neither is in §5.1's blocked set.
suggestion: State explicitly whether `runner`/`notify_cmd` are workflow fields or project-config-only keys; if they resolve layered, exclude the task-override and env layers for command-valued fields under `TP_UNATTENDED=1`, and add them to the §5.1 table.

finding: §8a's four field findings still carry no normative requirement anywhere in §3-§7 and §10: no changed behaviour, no exit code, no test. As written they cannot be decomposed into tasks — an implementer would have to infer both the fix and its acceptance. The section itself says review must fold them, and until it does, three of the four (next_action recommending an unhonourable registration, a truncated audit reporting complete, exit codes not separating a typo from a failure) directly affect the driver's own decisions.
suggestion: Fold each into a numbered requirement with a home: the merge overlap clustering into §4.1/§3.1 as a field of what the driver reads; the next_action check-phase guard into §4.1; the audit truncation into §3.3's audit-record unit with an explicit non-truncated total or a hard error; and the exit-code separation into a table of the codes tp run distinguishes, each with a matching test in §10.

finding: §8a's second routed finding rests on "**the driver is the consumer of `next_action`**, and an unattended run follows the recommendation with no human to catch it" — but §4.1 states the opposite design: `next_action` "stays the human-facing summary; `next_units` is what the driver consumes". Folded in as written, the finding would harden a consumption path §4.1 says does not exist, and if §4.1 is right the routed risk changes shape entirely (the recommendation reaches a human, not the loop).
suggestion: Resolve which object the driver reads before folding: if §4.1 stands, restate the §8a finding as "`next_action` misleads the operator reading `tp run --status`" and locate the fix accordingly; if the driver really does fall back to `next_action` when `next_units` is empty, say so in §4.1.

finding: Non-Goal 4 says 'No convergence policy changes … `tp run` obeys the resolved policy and never relaxes it', but §8a's accepted proposal changes the count of unresolved findings a location contributes ('the value is an honest count'). If that count is what `--status --check` and the convergence rule read, the honest count is a convergence policy change; if it is a second, display-only number, that must be said, or a driver will gate on the wrong one.
suggestion: When folding §8a in, state which number convergence gates on and which is reporting only, and amend Non-Goal 4 to exclude (or explicitly include) the clustering change.

finding: §1 promises that the divergence signal — `spec_coverage_clean_rounds`, `role_streaks`, `divergence` — 'travels in that report' so the operator gets it at the end of a run. §3.5's `--status` output is enumerated (phase, units done, spend against each cap, last unit's exit code and log path, `stop_reason`) and carries none of the three, and no other report is defined. The promise has no home, so no test can assert it.
suggestion: Add the three signals to the §3.5 `--status` field list for a run that stopped in the audit phase (or name the command that emits them), and add a test row asserting they appear on a non-converged audit stop.

finding: `args` offers a `{log_path}` placeholder while §3.5 says the driver itself streams each unit's runner output to `.tp/runs/<run-id>/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`. If tp owns the redirect, the placeholder is a second mechanism for the same file and invites a runner writing one path while tp writes another; if the runner owns it, tp is not streaming. `{unit_id}` is likewise unmotivated — no stated runner flag consumes it.
suggestion: Pick one owner of the log file and drop the other. Keep only placeholders a built-in template actually uses, and say so, since test 12 makes an unresolved placeholder a usage error.

finding: §3.2 pins the built-in `claude` template's mechanism in prose — print mode, streaming JSON output, `--permission-mode auto` — none of which the spec can establish as correct, and `auto` is not among the harness's documented permission modes. A wrong flag name here breaks the default runner while reading as settled design.
suggestion: Describe the template by requirement (non-interactive, machine-readable output, closed stdin, permissions pre-granted so no unit blocks on a prompt) and let the task's acceptance pin the exact flags against the installed harness version.

finding: Role units run 'parallel with sibling roles' with no ceiling: a 4- or 5-role corpus spawns that many agent processes at once, and the spec adds no run_max_concurrency field to §7. It is also unstated what happens when one sibling fails while others are still running — whether the driver kills the batch, waits for all, or retries only the failed unit before the record unit runs.
suggestion: Either state that concurrency equals the number of active roles by design and say why no ceiling is needed, or add a bounded-parallelism field; and define the batch failure policy (wait for all siblings, then retry only failed units, and never dispatch the record unit while any sibling is unfinished).

finding: §3.4 says "Every non-converged stop is a report to a human", yet `notify_cmd` is invoked only on `stop_reason: escalation` (§5.2). `cap-units`, `cap-wall-clock`, `cap-budget` and `unit-failure` end an overnight run just as silently as an escalation would have, and §7 defines `notify_cmd` generically with no such restriction.
suggestion: Invoke `notify_cmd` on every non-`converged` stop (and optionally on `converged` too), passing `stop_reason`, and say so once in §3.4 rather than only in §5.2.

finding: The plugin preflights and fails when tp is absent from PATH or 'older than the plugin's minimum', but the minimum version is never named, there is no stated place it is declared (plugin.json field?), and no detection mechanism is given (parsing tp --version output, and what to do when that parse fails).
suggestion: Declare the minimum version in a named plugin.json field, specify the detection command and comparison rule, and give the exact failure message including the install command and the treatment of an unparseable version.

finding: run_max_budget_usd is 0 (unbounded) with range 0-10000, but the numeric type is not stated (integer dollars? float? cents?) while every existing workflow field is an integer, and it is not said what {max_budget_usd} expands to when the value is 0. Test 12 makes an unresolved placeholder a usage error, so 'expand to nothing' needs to be an explicit rule rather than an implementer's choice.
suggestion: State the type and precision, and specify the unbounded expansion (e.g. the whole flag/value pair is dropped from the argv, which is not an unresolved placeholder) together with the same rule for {max_turns} when a runner has no turn cap.

finding: tp documents a per-field `--compact` disposition for every agent-facing field (REFERENCE.md §8.4: decision-critical survives, explanatory is omitted). This spec adds `next_units` to `tp resume --json` and `last_failure` to `tp resume`/`tp brief` and states no disposition for either, and §10 has no test for it — so the one output every fresh unit parses grows by an unstated amount even in compact mode.
suggestion: State the disposition explicitly: `next_units` survives `--compact` (decision-critical) minus any explanatory field; `last_failure.summary` is the candidate to strip. Add a test pinning the compact shape of both, as §10.1 already does for the object set.
